raw_response:
I'm a 55-year-old farmer with middle school education, been farming these 12 mu in Quzhou for 30 years now. My household has 10 people — my wife and I, my parents who are getting old, my two sons and their wives, and a couple of grandkids. Both my sons work off-farm, one in a factory in Shijiazhuang and one does construction in Handan. They send money home every month, which helps, but I still run the farm myself. I don't like asking them for money for inputs — this land is my responsibility.

With 10 people, I have plenty of family labor when I need it. My daughters-in-law help with planting and harvest, and even the grandkids can do some weeding. So I almost never hire labor unless it's an emergency. That saves me a lot of money.

I've been doing wheat-maize double cropping on these 12 mu for as long as I can remember. The extension agent came last year and talked about reducing fertilizer, saying we apply too much. I listened, but honestly, I've tried cutting back before and the yield dropped. I'd rather put down a bit more and make sure I don't have a bad year. Last year my wheat averaged about 450 kg/mu and maize about 500 kg/mu. The soil is decent but it's been worked hard for decades.

This year, I'll plant wheat in mid-October, right after I finish harvesting the late-season vegetables I tried on half a mu (not putting that in the main plan, it was an experiment). For the main 12 mu, I'll rotary till after clearing the fields, broadcast the seed and fertilizer, then drag a plank to cover everything. I buy improved wheat seed from the county supply store — about 15 kg per mu, costs me around 30 yuan per mu. I've learned not to buy cheap seed from the market. Five years ago I did that and got terrible germination, lost half a mu.

For fertilizer on wheat, I'll put down compound fertilizer before planting — about 50 kg per mu, which gives me roughly 15 kg N, 5 kg P, and 5 kg K per mu. Then at jointing in March, if the wheat looks a bit yellow or the weather has been dry, I'll topdress with urea, about 15 kg per mu. That extra application costs money but I've seen what happens when you skip it and April turns dry. You can't make up for it later. So all told, about 20 kg N per mu for wheat.

I'll irrigate wheat three times: once right after planting if it doesn't rain, once at jointing in March, and once at heading in April or May. The electricity for the well pump isn't cheap anymore — they meter it now — but wheat is my main cash crop and I can't afford to lose it to drought.

For maize, the window is always tight. I plant within two or three days of wheat harvest in early June. No time for fancy tillage — one quick pass with the rotary tiller if needed, then plant immediately. I use hybrid seed, about 45 yuan per mu. All the fertilizer goes in at planting — compound fertilizer in the furrow, about 45 kg per mu, plus a little urea. That's about 16 kg N, 4 kg P, 4 kg K total. No time for split application, the season is too short and the corn needs to get established before the summer heat.

I'll irrigate maize twice if the summer rains are scarce — usually once when it's knee-high in July and once at flowering in August. But if we get good rains, maybe only once. I watch the sky and decide.

For pesticides, I use herbicide on both crops — atrazine-type for maize, and a broadleaf herbicide for wheat. For maize I usually need one insecticide spray because the corn borer comes every year around July. I don't bother with fungicide unless I see disease, which is rare.

My total input costs this year will be around 5,200 yuan. That's seed, fertilizer, electricity for irrigation, and pesticides. I have the cash from my sons' remittances, so I won't need credit. My yield target is 460 kg/mu for wheat and 510 kg/mu for maize. If I hit those and prices hold, I'll do fine. Even if prices drop a bit, I'll have enough to cover costs and feed the family.
